clue.text: His brother Robert served with Thomas Hardy

definitions.text: His brother Robert served with Thomas Hardy

parts.words: His brother Robert served with Thomas Hardy
parts.note: in a Hardy novel the title soldier is John Loveday, whose brother Bob goes to sea with Captain Thomas Hardy on Nelson's Victory; the clue plays on Hardy as novelist and as sea captain

explanation.surface: A man's brother went to sea alongside the famous Captain Hardy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Thomas Hardy' reads as the novelist, but here he is also the captain of the Victory at Trafalgar, under whom the hero's sailor brother serves in the book.
explanation.definitionFit: The book's title character is a cavalry trumpeter whose sailor brother Bob serves at Trafalgar.

clue.text: Argonaut is heavyweight protecting backward chap

indicators.note: one piece guards another by wrapping round it, so the second goes inside the first

parts.note: a ton is a great weight

indicators.note: backward says the word for chap is written from right to left

parts.note: a chap is a male

explanation.surface: One of Jason's crew is a big man shielding a timid fellow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heavyweight' suggests a boxer, but it is just a large unit of weight; Telamon was the father of Ajax and sailed on the Argo.
explanation.definitionFit: Telamon, father of Ajax, sailed with Jason on the Argo in Greek myth.

clue.text: His old friend found love among his chickens

definitions.text: His old friend found love among his chickens

parts.words: His old friend found love among his chickens
parts.note: points to Wodehouse's novel Love Among the Chickens, in which the narrator, an old friend of the chicken-farming schemer, falls in love

explanation.surface: A pal visiting a poultry farm ended up falling in love there.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase 'love among his chickens' is nearly the title of the Wodehouse novel about a disastrous chicken farm run by this character.
explanation.definitionFit: Stanley Featherstonehaugh Ukridge is Wodehouse's chicken-farming chancer whose friend narrates the novel.

clue.text: "Though even the word Marsala will smack of preciosity / Soon in the —— West." (D. H. Lawrence, Birds, Beasts and Flowers)

definitions.text: "Though even the word Marsala will smack of preciosity / Soon in the —— West." (D. H. Lawrence, Birds, Beasts and Flowers)

parts.words: "Though even the word Marsala will smack of preciosity / Soon in the —— West." (D. H. Lawrence, Birds, Beasts and Flowers)
parts.note: a quotation with a gap: Lawrence mocks an American West gone dry under Prohibition, nicknamed after the temperance campaigner William Johnson

explanation.walkthrough: The missing word is the nickname of the American prohibitionist William E. Johnson, applied to the teetotal West where even naming a wine sounds affected.
explanation.definitionFit: The temperance crusader William Johnson's nickname came to stand for teetotalism, so the dry West is described with it.

clue.text: It goes on ahead in question Portia raises …

indicators.note: in says the answer sits inside the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: Portia raises a point under discussion about something that goes forward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'question' links this to the next clue's casket test in The Merchant of Venice; the letters lie across 'Portia raises'. 'goes on ahead' means is worn on the head.
explanation.definitionFit: A jewelled crown is worn on the head, so it goes on a head.

clue.text: … he showed a preference for silver in Belmont

definitions.text: … he showed a preference for silver in Belmont

parts.words: … he showed a preference for silver in Belmont
parts.note: in The Merchant of Venice Portia's suitors at Belmont choose among gold, silver and lead caskets; one prince picks silver

explanation.surface: A man at Belmont preferred silver to the other choices.
explanation.walkthrough: Belmont is Portia's estate; of her suitors, Morocco picks gold, this prince silver and Bassanio lead.
explanation.definitionFit: The Prince of Arragon is the suitor who chooses the silver casket and loses Portia.

clue.text: Playwright from royal house?

definitions.meaning: John ... wrote Look Back in Anger
Queen Victoria's seaside home on the Isle of Wight was a royal residence

explanation.surface: A dramatist emerging from a palace.
explanation.definitionFit: John Osborne was the dramatist, and Victoria's Isle of Wight retreat bears the same name.

clue.text: Frank Scott narrator

parts.note: Frank is the first name of the young man who tells the story of Scott's Rob Roy, not an adjective meaning candid

explanation.surface: An honest storyteller called Scott.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Frank' looks like an adjective, candid, but it is the narrator's first name in Walter Scott's Rob Roy.
explanation.definitionFit: Frank Osbaldistone narrates Walter Scott's novel Rob Roy.

clue.text: Sailors miscast in Tarkovsky classic

indicators.note: miscast says the letters of the word sailors are cast into a different order

explanation.surface: Sea-going actors are badly chosen for a famous Russian film.
explanation.walkthrough: 'miscast' rearranges SAILORS.
explanation.definitionFit: Andrei Tarkovsky's 1972 science-fiction film is set on a space station above an ocean planet.

clue.text: He went from the absurd to panic — but only in play

definitions.text: He went from the absurd to panic — but only in play

parts.words: He went from the absurd to panic — but only in play
parts.note: a Spanish dramatist moved from the Theatre of the Absurd to founding the Panic Movement, a playful pun on panic as alarm

explanation.surface: A man moved from silliness to alarm, though only as a game.
explanation.walkthrough: The Panic Movement, named for the god Pan, was founded in 1962 by this dramatist with Jodorowsky and Topor; 'only in play' says the panic was theatrical.
explanation.definitionFit: Fernando Arrabal wrote absurdist drama and then co-founded the Panic Movement in Paris.

clue.text: Hotspur would have had his wife emulate her singing

definitions.text: Hotspur would have had his wife emulate her singing

parts.words: Hotspur would have had his wife emulate her singing
parts.note: in Henry IV Part 1 a Welsh-speaking wife sings, and Hotspur teases his own wife Kate to sing too

explanation.surface: A hothead wanted his wife to sing like another woman.
explanation.walkthrough: Hotspur is the fiery Harry Percy in Shakespeare's Henry IV Part 1; Glendower's daughter, married to Mortimer, sings in Welsh.
explanation.definitionFit: Glendower's daughter, wife to Mortimer, sings a Welsh song in Henry IV Part 1.

clue.text: Evil spirit (like Monday — nothing new there!)

parts.note: as means like

indicators.note: there is no new, so the abbreviation N for new is removed from the day

explanation.surface: A demon, about as welcome as the start of the working week, offers nothing fresh.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nothing new there' takes N (new) out of MONDAY, leaving MODAY.
explanation.definitionFit: Asmoday is a form of Asmodeus, a demon of Jewish and occult lore.

clue.text: Some change Redgauntlet, already filled with rage

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Altering Scott's novel Redgauntlet would provoke an already furious reader.
explanation.walkthrough: Redgauntlet is a Walter Scott novel; the letters run from 'change' into its name.
explanation.definitionFit: Being made furious is a synonym for being full of rage.

clue.text: Poet finished about noon

indicators.note: about says the word for finished goes round the other piece

parts.note: finished means done

explanation.surface: A poet completed his work around midday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts N inside DONE.
explanation.definitionFit: John Donne was the metaphysical poet and Dean of St Paul's.

clue.text: The Prince of Storytellers offers work to writer on German home

parts.note: op, short for opus, is a work
a pen is a writing instrument
Heim is German for home

explanation.surface: A celebrated storyteller gives a job to an author living in a German house.
explanation.walkthrough: E. Phillips Oppenheim, the prolific thriller writer, was billed as 'the Prince of Storytellers'.
explanation.definitionFit: The popular novelist E. Phillips Oppenheim was marketed under that grand title.

clue.text: Heretics suggest mutiny of characters in angry ship

indicators.note: the letters revolt against their places, as a crew rises up, so they are reordered

explanation.surface: Dissenters stir up a revolt among the crew of a furious vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mutiny of characters in' rearranges ANGRY SHIP.
explanation.definitionFit: Early Montanists were called Phrygians after their homeland and were condemned by the Church.

clue.text: Second show of amusement for thriller writer

parts.note: laughter shows amusement

explanation.surface: A second burst of mirth goes to a crime novelist.
explanation.definitionFit: Karin Slaughter is an American author of crime thrillers.

clue.text: His rehearsal was as good as a play

definitions.text: His rehearsal was as good as a play

parts.words: His rehearsal was as good as a play
parts.note: a French dramatist wrote a play called The Rehearsal, La Répétition, so his rehearsal truly was a play

explanation.surface: A man's practice run was as entertaining as a real show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'as good as a play' is an idiom for entertaining; here the rehearsal literally is a play, Jean Anouilh's La Répétition.
explanation.definitionFit: Jean Anouilh, the French playwright, wrote La Répétition ou l'Amour puni.

clue.text: Argue it hopelessly to show French writer

indicators.note: hopelessly says the letters of argue it are muddled into a new order

explanation.surface: Debate a point without hope of winning to bring out a Frenchman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hopelessly' rearranges ARGUE IT.
explanation.definitionFit: Théophile Gautier was a French poet and novelist.

clue.text: Ironic interpretation, say, of old goat

indicators.note: say signals that the word for ironic interpretation is spoken, giving a word that sounds the same

parts.note: a satire mocks through irony

explanation.surface: A mocking reading of an elderly goat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' asks for a sound-alike of SATIRE. 'old goat' suits the goat-legged satyr and the lecherous old man.
explanation.definitionFit: A satyr is a lustful goat-legged woodland god, and an 'old goat' is a lecher.

clue.text: Charles Johnson's pseudonymous protagonist

parts.note: the central figure of a work by Charles Johnson goes under an assumed title rather than her own name

explanation.surface: A hero who hides behind a false name in a Charles Johnson story.
explanation.definitionFit: The heroine of Charles Johnson's work is known by a title meaning a sultan's consort rather than her real name.

clue.text: Conrad makes short work of a severe attack of wind

definitions.meaning: Joseph Conrad wrote a novella, a short work, named after a storm at sea
a violent tropical storm in the western Pacific

explanation.surface: A novelist quickly sees off a bad bout of flatulence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'makes short work of' looks like dispatching something fast; read as 'Conrad's short work' it is his 1902 novella.
explanation.definitionFit: Conrad's 1902 novella is named for a tropical cyclone, the kind of storm the second definition means.

clue.text: "Wordsworthians were there to discover the hallmark of genius on his most insignificant ities" (John Middleton Murry, The Problem of Style)

definitions.text: "Wordsworthians were there to discover the hallmark of genius on his most insignificant ities" (John Middleton Murry, The Problem of Style)

parts.words: "Wordsworthians were there to discover the hallmark of genius on his most insignificant ities" (John Middleton Murry, The Problem of Style)
parts.note: a quotation with a word cut short: the missing start, joined to the printed ending, makes a noun for pompous, booming pronouncements

explanation.walkthrough: The gap is the front of a word whose printed ending '-ities' completes it; the light holds only that front part, an adjective for a full, pompous style.
explanation.definitionFit: Murry mocks admirers who found genius even in Wordsworth's most grandiloquent, sonorous trifles.

clue.text: He was associated with archangel to identify fellow poet

definitions.text: He was associated with archangel to identify fellow poet

parts.words: He was associated with archangel to identify fellow poet
parts.note: a Victorian painter-poet was named Gabriel Charles followed by the great Italian's name, and that name sits beside the archangel's

explanation.surface: A man linked with an archangel helps to pick out another poet.
explanation.walkthrough: Dante Gabriel Rossetti put the Italian poet's name beside the archangel Gabriel's, identifying himself with a fellow poet.
explanation.definitionFit: The Florentine poet's name joins the archangel's in Dante Gabriel Rossetti.

clue.text: Browning remarked his touch on the clavichord

definitions.text: Browning remarked his touch on the clavichord

parts.words: Browning remarked his touch on the clavichord
parts.note: Robert Browning's poem A Toccata of an eighteenth-century Venetian composer considers his keyboard music

explanation.surface: A poet commented on a musician's keyboard technique.
explanation.walkthrough: Browning's poem is 'A Toccata of Galuppi's'; Baldassare Galuppi was a Venetian composer.
explanation.definitionFit: Baldassare Galuppi is the Venetian composer of the toccata in Browning's poem.

clue.text: Publication I found with it in East River

indicators.note: in says the first person and the pronoun sit inside the river's name

parts.note: the Don is a river in Russia and in England
taken as written

explanation.surface: A book appears, with me and it placed in an eastern river.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads I and IT before the river, but they are set inside it; 'found with' only links the first person to the pronoun.
explanation.definitionFit: An edition is a printed issue of a book or paper, one form of publication.

clue.text: Mystical interpretation of a Greek tempo

parts.note: an is the indefinite article, a form of a
agoge is the Greek term for tempo or rhythmic movement in music

explanation.surface: A spiritual reading of the pace of Greek music.
explanation.walkthrough: Agoge, in ancient Greek music theory, is tempo.
explanation.definitionFit: Anagoge is the spiritual sense of scripture, a mystical reading beyond the literal.

clue.text: He was given his own way by Scott Moncrieff

definitions.text: He was given his own way by Scott Moncrieff

parts.words: He was given his own way by Scott Moncrieff
parts.note: C. K. Scott Moncrieff translated Proust's first volume as a title naming a character's own way

explanation.surface: A man was allowed to do as he pleased by a translator.
explanation.walkthrough: 'given his own way' looks like being indulged, but Scott Moncrieff's English title for Proust's first volume is Swann's Way.
explanation.definitionFit: Proust's character Charles Swann gives his name to Scott Moncrieff's title Swann's Way.
